Engagement 07  ·  Infrastructure Design Review Fix the Design While It Is Cheap.

Four requirements, checked at six layers. Every requirement appears in more than one layer, which is why a checklist misses them. You leave with target-state options, their trade-offs, and a migration sequence in dependency order.

4–6 weeksSovereign infrastructurePre-build or in-flight
Request a design review

What this is

Infrastructure Design Review

An infrastructure design review tests a proposed or existing architecture against four requirements — data residency, resilience, AI-readiness, and cryptographic posture — across every layer from physical siting to application. It produces findings, a risk register, target-state options, and a migration sequence before the design is committed to.

Deliverables

What You Get

01

Requirement-to-Layer Matrix

Four requirements assessed at six layers, with a finding recorded in every cell that carries one.

02

Design Findings

Each with the requirement it affects, the layer it sits in, and the consequence if unaddressed.

03

Risk Register

Ordered by consequence, with owners and the decision each risk requires.

04

Target-State Options

Two or three viable architectures with cost, complexity, and residency trade-offs stated.

05

Cryptographic Posture Assessment

Whether the estate can be enumerated, and whether the design permits an algorithm change without a rebuild.

06

Migration Sequence

Dependency-ordered, with the decisions that gate each step identified.

Questions We Are Asked

Can you review a design before we build it?
That is the intended use. The review is most valuable at the point where the architecture is decided and least valuable after procurement has been committed, because most of the findings are cheap at design time and expensive to retrofit.
What does AI-ready infrastructure actually mean?
That the estate can carry AI workloads without being rebuilt twice. Practically: the data is where the compute can reach it at acceptable latency, the bandwidth between them is sized for the workload, there is a deployment pattern for inference, and sensitive workloads have an isolation model that does not depend on a promise.
Do you assess post-quantum readiness?
Yes, as part of cryptographic posture. The assessment covers whether the cryptographic estate can be enumerated at all — which is the first deliverable in any migration — and whether the design supports changing an algorithm or key length without rebuilding dependent systems.
Will you also build what you recommend?
Orvix designs and reviews. It does not operate the infrastructure it designs, and where an assurance opinion is needed over a design Orvix authored, that opinion is written by an independent party. That boundary is stated before the engagement starts, not discovered at the end of it.
How is this different from a cloud well-architected review?
A well-architected review assesses a workload against a provider's own framework. This review assesses a design against four requirements that cut across providers — residency, resilience, AI-readiness, and cryptographic posture — and it is run by a party with no interest in which provider is chosen.
